Let us review Architectural Decision Record 130 concerning the persistent storage backend for our IoT telemetry ingestion pipeline. Currently, our write throughput spikes to 45000 incoming sensor events per second, which causes severe write amplification and lock contention on our existing Postgres cluster. Under this proposal, we migrate the raw time-series storage to ScyllaDB, while retaining Postgres strictly for relational metadata and device authentication records.

ScyllaDB uses a share-nothing thread-per-core architecture implemented in C++, which matches our hardware profiles and avoids Java garbage collection pauses. We configure a replication factor of 3 across 9 storage nodes with local quorum write consistency. Benchmark tests demonstrate that write latency drops from 30 milliseconds down to 4 milliseconds at the P99 threshold, handling up to 2000000 records per minute without buffer exhaustion.

Previously, different engineering teams published arbitrary JSON payloads to shared topics, causing downstream consumer deserialization crashes whenever fields were renamed. Under this ADR, every event schema must be registered in the Confluent schema registry using Apache Avro before deploying producer services.

We establish full compatibility mode as the default enforcement policy, ensuring older consumers can process payloads produced by newer schemas. We cap individual message payload size at 1 megabyte and enforce a retention period of 7 days on raw event partitions, while critical financial audit topics utilize compacted topic retention.

We currently operate 5 Consul clusters, but face frequent operational friction around snapshot management and gossip protocol split-brain scenarios during WAN network partitions. This RFC proposes consolidating our cluster coordination and dynamic configuration store on etcd version 3.

In Architectural Decision Record 216, we define the distributed tracing context propagation standard across 75 backend microservices. Our investigation revealed that inconsistent tracing headers resulted in fragmented call graphs where child spans failed to link back to the originating span. We mandate the W3C trace context specification as the sole standard for all outgoing HTTP and gRPC headers.

Each service extracts traceparent headers at the ingress boundary and propagates the span context across internal asynchronous tasks. We configure head-based sampling at the originating span with a sampling rate of 10 percent for standard user traffic, while capturing 100 percent of synthetic health checks and transactions that return error status codes. This strategy preserves trace visibility across 500 microservice endpoints while preventing storage saturation in our tracing backend.

Let us review technical RFC 230 concerning multi-region deployment and active-active failover architecture. Evaluating active-active writes across 2 geographic regions revealed significant complexity around asynchronous conflict resolution and distributed locking under high transaction concurrency. We therefore adopt an active-passive architecture with an active primary region in US East and a warm standby in US West.

The primary relational database streams changes asynchronously to the secondary region, with cross-region replication lag monitored at less than 500 milliseconds. In the event of an unrecoverable regional outage, automated failover promotes the secondary replica within 3 minutes by rerouting global domain name system traffic via health-checked Anycast latency policies. This approach meets our recovery point objective of 30 seconds and recovery time objective of 5 minutes.
